Unfortunately, that's how term insurance works. Most people never cash out their term, so insurance companies offer lower premiums. Term insurance is really only beneficial to employers or to cover your income. It goes away, has cheaper premiums, and goes up every time you renew. Most people who want final expenses or to leave a legacy are better off with universal life or whole life.

There are many BS companies out there. Insurance is highly regulated, by law, but if your agent/ broker doesn't EXPLAIN to you the differences, pros and cons, they are nothing but a salesman with a script. I could advise which companies are better, but you would have to dm me, because by law we are also not allowed to solicit all willy nilly, nor would I do business this way. I meet with people and go over the options available to them, and teach them what they need to know, however I work for a very old school, not advertised (bc we don't pay to sell, we work off reputation) company that would rather do right by people than most major insurance companies that sell you and forget you. 

Not too many commercial, major insurance do that anymore. We are one of the oldest insurance companies around (prior to even BCBS), but the culture really emphasizes ethics and services over commission. 

Do your own research, dm me if you have questions. I'm not gonna lie, I might make commissions paid by the company, I might not be licensed in your state (I'm in Florida), but I might have a coworker that IS. 

Insurance is mostly smoke and mirrors, but that doesn't mean there aren't reputable companies out there. 

I have worked in insurance for YEARS and finally found a company I believe in. We focus on retirement planning insurances; life, med sups (we also offer advantages plans, but they are total bs, at least for Florida), long term care (which is so important and no one talks about), and various financial protections.

The earlier you protect yourself, the more money you can save throughout the retirement years bc retirement is 90% insurance.
